summary: Defines the Port Control Protocol, which lets an IPv4 or IPv6 host control how incoming packets are translated and forwarded by a NAT or simple firewall. It also lets a host reduce its outgoing NAT keepalive messages.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer behind a gate politely asks the gatekeeper to let certain visitors in and to remember them without constant check-ins.

subtitle: A protocol that lets a host ask its NAT or firewall to open, keep and report port mappings, instead of guessing or sending constant keepalives.

tldr.problem: Hosts behind a NAT or firewall cannot receive inbound connections without a mapping, and applications waste bandwidth and battery on keepalive messages to stop NATs from forgetting their sessions.
tldr.mechanism: PCP is a UDP request/response protocol in which a client asks a PCP server on the NAT or firewall to create, renew or delete mappings using the MAP and PEER Opcodes, and learns the lifetime it was granted.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can run servers behind NATs, including carrier-grade NATs and IPv6 firewalls, and can send fewer keepalives. RFC 6887 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 7488, RFC 7652 and RFC 7843.

today: RFC 6887 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7488, RFC 7652 and RFC 7843, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: What PCP Is For
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP) controls how incoming packets are forwarded by upstream devices such as NAT64, NAT44 and IPv4 and IPv6 firewalls, and it reduces application keepalive traffic. It is designed for Carrier-Grade NATs (CGNs), small residential NATs, and dual-stack and IPv6-only CPE routers. It lets a host run a server for a long time (a home security camera) or a short time (a game or a phone call) behind a NAT.

PCP applications create mappings from an external IP address, protocol and port to an internal IP address, protocol and port. PCP does not tell remote computers about the new address. That rendezvous step stays application specific, for example a game's own server, a SIP proxy, or DNS Update.

Many applications also send frequent NAT keepalive messages so a NAT does not time out their session. By learning and influencing the mapping lifetime through PCP, they can send these less often, saving access-network bandwidth, server traffic and mobile battery. The RFC also notes that Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) in NATs have been detrimental to protocol evolution, and PCP lets applications create their own mappings, reducing the incentive to deploy ALGs.

PCP assumes a single-homed model: for a given host IP address there is only one default route out. The reply to an inbound packet has to pass back through the same NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: If you live behind a locked gate, friends cannot knock on your door unless the gatekeeper knows about them. PCP is a way to tell the gatekeeper who may come in and for how long, so you do not have to keep waving at the gate to stay on the list.

sections.title: Design: Hints Up, Notifications Down
sections.content:
The RFC defines a PCP client (software that sends requests), a PCP server (software on or controlling the NAT or firewall) and a PCP-controlled device (the NAT or firewall itself). The server is normally part of the NAT or firewall, but it can be a separate device as long as clients cannot tell the difference.

Mappings come in kinds. Implicit dynamic mappings appear as a side effect of traffic such as an outgoing TCP SYN. Explicit dynamic mappings are made by PCP MAP and PEER requests and have a lifetime that the client must renew, like a DHCP lease. Explicit static mappings are configured by hand and last until removed.

The RFC suggests viewing PCP as a stream of hints from client to server (what the client would like) and a stream of notifications from server to client (what the state actually is). That is why retransmissions and renewals are the same packet on the wire, and why there is no transaction ID. A server response is self-describing, and a client can ignore a notification for a mapping it does not want.

PCP always uses fixed 128-bit address fields. An IPv4 address is stored as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, and all of the first 96 bits MUST be checked when testing for one.
sections.plainLanguage: The client keeps telling the gatekeeper what it wants, and the gatekeeper keeps telling the client what it really did. They do not need to number every note, because each note says everything on its own.

sections.title: The PCP Message Format
sections.content:
All PCP messages are sent over UDP, with a maximum UDP payload of 1100 octets. A message has a common header, an Opcode-specific part and zero or more options. Numbers larger than one octet are in network byte order.

A request header holds Version (2), an R bit (0 for request, 1 for response), a 7-bit Opcode, 16 reserved bits, a 32-bit Requested Lifetime in seconds, and the 128-bit PCP Client's IP Address. That last field repeats the source address so the server can detect an unexpected NAT between client and server; if it does not match, the server returns ADDRESS_MISMATCH.

A response header replaces the request's lifetime with a Result Code and has a Lifetime (the mapping lifetime on success, or how long the same error should be expected on failure) and a 32-bit Epoch Time, followed by 96 reserved bits. Error responses copy the request, up to 1100 octets, with the result code set.

Options use a type-length-value layout: an 8-bit code, 8 reserved bits and a 16-bit length, padded to a multiple of 4 octets. If the high bit of the code is 0, the option is mandatory to process; if it is 1, the server MAY ignore it. An error leaves the server and the controlled device unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Every PCP note starts with the same small form: what kind of note it is, how long you want the favor to last, and your own address so the gatekeeper can check you are who you say you are.

sections.title: Client and Server Operation
sections.content:
A client finds its server from configuration (for example DHCP) or, failing that, its default router list. The client picks a random source port, and the server only accepts normal requests on the interface facing the internal network, silently ignoring those on other interfaces. Every request generates at least one response, so PCP needs no reliable transport.

The client is responsible for retransmission. Initial retransmission time SHOULD be 3 seconds and the maximum retransmission time SHOULD be 1024 seconds. Each timeout doubles the previous one, with a random factor between -0.1 and +0.1. Retransmissions reuse the same Mapping Nonce.

Every response carries an Epoch Time that increments once per second. If the server loses its mapping state, or its external address changes, it MUST reset the Epoch. A client that sees the value go backwards, or grow at a rate that does not match its own clock, concludes that the server probably lost state and promptly renews its mappings. The check tolerates up to 1/16 (6.25%) clock difference.

Rapid recovery shortens the time before clients notice. A server that can lose state or change mappings MUST implement either the ANNOUNCE Opcode or Mapping Update, and SHOULD implement both. After a restart, a server can multicast an ANNOUNCE to 224.0.0.1 or ff02::1 on UDP port 5350, and clients wait a random 0 to 5 seconds before recreating their mappings. With Mapping Update, a server that remembers its state sends an unsolicited MAP or PEER response carrying the new external address and port.

Servers listen for requests on UDP port 5351. Clients listen for multicast announcements on 5350, a separate port because one device may be both a server and a client.
sections.plainLanguage: If the gatekeeper does not answer, the client asks again, waiting longer each time. The gatekeeper also keeps a clock that restarts at zero if it forgets everyone, so clients can notice and remind it.

sections.title: The MAP and PEER Opcodes
sections.content:
The Opcodes defined here are ANNOUNCE (0), MAP (1) and PEER (2). They are designed for transport protocols with 16-bit ports such as TCP, UDP, SCTP and DCCP.

MAP creates an explicit dynamic inbound mapping so that a listening server can be reached. The request holds a 96-bit random Mapping Nonce, a protocol, an internal port, and a suggested external port and address. A zero in the suggestions means no preference. The client MUST assume it may never get the external port it suggests. The server returns the assigned external address and port and a lifetime. A requested lifetime of 0 deletes the mapping, and under the Simple Threat Model a request for an existing mapping with a different nonce is rejected with NOT_AUTHORIZED. Protocol 0 with port 0 means all traffic (a "DMZ host").

PEER manages an outbound mapping to a given remote peer, identified by a five-tuple of protocol, internal address and port, and remote peer address and port. A client uses it to learn or extend the lifetime of the mapping a NAT made for an existing connection, which is how an application reduces keepalives. It can also recreate a mapping after the NAT loses state. PEER cannot shorten a lifetime or delete a mapping.

A client renews a mapping by sending the same request again, with the currently assigned address and port as the suggestions, at a random time between 1/2 and 5/8 of the way to expiry. Renewal requests MUST NOT be sent less than four seconds apart. A server SHOULD be configurable with minimum and maximum lifetimes, with a minimum of 120 seconds and the maximum, if no better information exists, 24 hours. In the simple security model a PCP request MUST NOT cause a mapping to expire sooner than it naturally would have, which prevents an attacker from forcing early reassignment of a port.
sections.plainLanguage: MAP says "please let visitors in at this door". PEER says "I already called this friend, so please keep our phone line open for longer". Either way, you have to ask again before your time runs out.

sections.title: Options for MAP and PEER
sections.content:
Three options are defined in this document.

  • THIRD_PARTY (code 1) lets a client control a mapping for another internal host. It MUST NOT be implemented or used unless the network carrying the PCP messages is fully trusted, and customer premises equipment is RECOMMENDED to prohibit it by default.
  • PREFER_FAILURE (code 2, MAP only) tells the server not to create a mapping at all if it cannot use the suggested external port and address, and to return CANNOT_PROVIDE_EXTERNAL. It exists for interworking with protocols such as UPnP IGDv1, and other clients SHOULD NOT use it. PEER implies this behaviour automatically.
  • FILTER (code 3, MAP only) names a remote peer address prefix and port that may send packets in, and the device drops the rest. A prefix length of 0 removes all filters. All PCP servers MUST support at least one filter per mapping.

The FILTER option is described as a performance optimization, useful to battery-powered wireless devices because they do not have to wake up just to reject unwanted traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Options are extra notes stapled to the request: "I am asking for my brother", "only this exact door or nothing", and "only let in people from this street".

sections.title: Threat Models and Security
sections.content:
PCP's security goal is to avoid new denial-of-service opportunities and unauthorized changes to mappings. Unauthorized changes can lead to traffic theft. The RFC defines two models.

The Simple Threat Model protects against off-path attackers. It does not defend against attackers who can modify, drop or inject spoofed packets on the internal side. A server stays secure under it if it configures no explicit mapping that it would not also configure implicitly: for example, explicit mappings get the same lifetime as implicit ones, hosts share one administrative domain, and THIRD_PARTY is not supported.

The Advanced Threat Model is needed for equipment such as corporate firewalls, CGNs serving several administrative domains, or anything more permissive for explicit mappings than implicit ones. It would need a PCP security mechanism that gives an authenticated, integrity-protected signaling channel. This RFC does not specify one.

Residual threats include quota exhaustion, on-path attackers who drop or spoof responses (no mitigation is offered), and spoofed source addresses, so ingress filtering (RFC 2827) SHOULD be used between hosts and the server. Servers SHOULD keep per-host or per-subscriber mapping quotas. A mapping may be taken by another host between a server losing state and a client noticing the Epoch change. Rapid recovery shortens that window but does not remove it. The RFC does not specify server discovery beyond contacting the default gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The gatekeeper has to be careful that nobody pretends to be you and takes your visitors. PCP protects against strangers far away, but if a bad person is standing right at your gate, it cannot stop them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
PCP uses UDP ports 5350 and 5351, which IANA reassigned from NAT-PMP (RFC 6886) to PCP. A PCP server MUST NOT create client mappings for external UDP ports 5350 or 5351.

IANA created three registries. Opcodes run from 0 to 127, with 0 ANNOUNCE, 1 MAP and 2 PEER and the rest allocated by Standards Action or Specification Required, or reserved for private use. Result codes run from 0 to 255 and start with the codes in the RFC. Options run from 0 to 255, with 0 to 127 mandatory to process and 128 to 255 optional.

The RFC also describes a transition from NAT-PMP: a server that answers with version number zero in an UNSUPP_VERSION response is a NAT-PMP server, and a client MAY then use the older protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number keepers set aside two door numbers and three lists for PCP, so that new kinds of requests can be added later without clashing.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: PCP Client's IP Address
fields.desc: Source address used by the client; IPv4 is IPv4-mapped. Used to detect an unexpected NAT.

items.label: UNSUPP_VERSION
items.desc: Server does not recognize the version.

items.label: NOT_AUTHORIZED
items.desc: Operation disabled or against server policy.

items.label: MALFORMED_OPTION
items.desc: Option appears too many times or has a bad length.

items.label: NETWORK_FAILURE
items.desc: Server or device has a network failure.

items.label: NO_RESOURCES
items.desc: Valid request, but not enough resources now.

items.label: USER_EX_QUOTA
items.desc: Would exceed the subscriber's port quota.

items.label: CANNOT_PROVIDE_EXTERNAL
items.desc: Suggested external port or address cannot be provided.

items.label: ADDRESS_MISMATCH
items.desc: Source address differs from the client address field.

items.label: EXCESSIVE_REMOTE_PEERS
items.desc: Filters in a MAP request could not be created.

items.title: ANNOUNCE (0)
items.text: No payload. Used for restart announcements and to read the server's Epoch without changing state.

items.title: MAP (1)
items.text: Creates, renews or deletes an explicit inbound mapping so a host can accept connections.

items.title: PEER (2)
items.text: Creates or extends an outbound mapping to one remote peer, to cut keepalives or recreate state.
